title: Vendor Access, Secrets Handling, and Endpoint Hardening Addendum (VASEH Addendum)
summary: Draft addendum that can be attached to vendor contracts and DPAs to define minimum acceptable practices for vendor access, secrets lifecycle, and endpoint hardening for private and on-prem deployments.
content:
Purpose and scope:
This addendum ("VASEH Addendum") supplements existing agreements (including Master Services Agreements and Data Processing Agreements) between Redwood Inference ("Customer") and Vendor ("Vendor"). It sets minimum technical, procedural, and audit obligations for vendor personnel, services, and software components that: (a) access Customer data, (b) operate in Customer-controlled infrastructure (VPCs, on-prem racks), or (c) run in hybrid environments where secrets or keys are provisioned into vendor-managed agents.

Applicability:
- Applies to any engagement where Vendor requires: remote access to Customer environments, installation or operation of agent software, persistence of Customer secrets on vendor systems, or the ability to modify runtime configuration of private deployments.
- Does not replace application- or project-specific security requirements; those may introduce stricter controls which prevail.

Definitions (key):
- "Secrets": any credential, key, token, certificate, or other sensitive material used to authenticate, authorize, or encrypt data or services.
- "Customer Environment": VPCs, dedicated clusters, on-prem servers/appliances, or other infrastructure under Customer control or custody.
- "Vendor Personnel": employees, contractors, or subcontractors of the Vendor who have access to Customer systems or data.
- "Privileged Access": access that allows configuration, administrative operations, or retrieval of secrets/keys or access to raw Customer data.

Core obligations:
1) Principle of least privilege and just-in-time access:
   - Vendor shall enforce least privilege for all accounts with access to Customer Environments. Privileged access must be granted only after an approval workflow and for the minimum time required.
   - All privileged sessions must use ephemeral credentials or just-in-time privilege elevation that expires automatically.

2) Secrets handling, storage, and transmission:
   - Persistent storage of Customer secrets by Vendor on shared or vendor-managed persistent volumes is prohibited unless explicitly authorized by written schedule.
   - Where secrets must be present, they must be stored using Customer-managed KMS or HSM when available. If Customer KMS/HSM is not available, Vendor-managed KMS is permitted only if encrypted keys are wrapped with Customer-controlled root keys and the Customer has the ability to revoke keys and access.
   - All secrets in transit must use TLS 1.2+ with modern cipher suites; mutual TLS is required for service-to-service communications that cross trust boundaries.
   - Secrets must not be logged in plaintext in any logs, monitoring systems, or error traces.

3) Key rotation and compromise handling:
   - Vendor must support automated key rotation at configurable intervals. Rotation must be capable of being initiated by the Customer.
   - If a secret compromise is suspected or confirmed, Vendor must notify Customer within 4 hours and provide a technical incident report and remediation plan within 48 hours.

4) Endpoint hardening and agent requirements:
   - Any vendor agent or software installed in a Customer Environment must run with non-root privileges, have an auditable install process, and be capable of being disabled/removed by Customer without vendor intervention.
   - Agents must enforce process isolation, validate code signatures for updates, and perform local integrity checks on startup. Automatic updates must be signed and allow offline verification.

5) Access controls, MFA, and SSO integration:
   - Vendor Personnel must authenticate via SSO supporting SAML 2.0/OIDC integrated with Customer identity where required. Multifactor authentication (MFA) is mandatory for any account with privileged access.
   - Shared or generic accounts are prohibited. Where machine identities are necessary, they must be issued per-instance, tied to lifecycle, and centrally managed.

6) Audit, logging, and traceability:
   - Vendor must maintain immutable audit logs for all privileged operations and access to secrets; logs must contain identity, source IP, timestamp, action, and session identifiers.
   - Logs relevant to Customer data access or secrets handling must be retained for a minimum of 1 year (or as required by applicable law) and be exportable to Customer SIEM on request.

7) Vulnerability management and secure SDLC:
   - Vendor shall maintain a documented vulnerability management program with defined SLA windows for remediation by severity (Critical: 72 hours, High: 14 days, Medium: 30 days, Low: next maintenance cycle).
   - Agents or binaries installed in Customer Environments must be produced from an auditable build pipeline, signed, and have reproducible build metadata available to Customer upon request.

8) Pen testing and independent assessments:
   - Annual third-party penetration testing of vendor components that interact with Customer Environments is required. Results and remediation summaries must be provided to Customer under NDA.
   - For on-prem or air-gapped deployments, Customer has the right to commission additional testing; Vendor cooperation and timely access must be arranged under mutually agreed terms.

9) Subprocessors and third-party services:
   - Vendor must maintain a subprocessors registry and provide notice of any changes 30 days in advance. High-risk subprocessors (hosting providers, KMS vendors, MSPs with privileged access) must be approved by Customer.

10) Data handling, deletion, and proof of destruction:
   - For secrets and key material, Vendor must support immediate revocation workflows and provide cryptographic evidence of deletion (where feasible) or an attestation describing deletion processes and timelines.
   - Upon termination or decommissioning of an environment, Vendor must provide an inventory of secrets and confirm secure deletion of all Customer secrets from vendor-managed storage within 30 days unless retention is required by law.

11) Onsite access and physical security (for appliance/on-prem models):
   - Any physical access to Customer-controlled hardware by Vendor Personnel requires preapproval, an escort by Customer-designated staff, and on-site identity verification. Physical keys, console access, or BIOS-level credentials must be under Customer control unless otherwise agreed.

12) Incident response, forensics, and transparency:
   - Vendor must integrate into Customer incident response playbooks for incidents that affect Customer data or keys. Joint warroom access and technical points of contact must be available 24/7 during active incidents.
   - Vendor will preserve forensic evidence and supply a chain-of-custody and all relevant logs to Customer or an independent investigator as requested.

13) Metrics and SLAs for access and secrets services:
   - Availability of critical control plane APIs (e.g., KMS endpoints, agent management) must be contractually defined. Vendor must provide uptime metrics and SLO reports monthly.

14) Exceptions and change control:
   - Any deviation from the Addendum requires written exception signed by authorized security representatives from both parties and must include compensating controls and a defined expiration.

Sample contract clause (technical annex excerpt):
"Vendor shall not persist Customer secrets or credentials in cleartext in vendor-managed shared storage. All secrets deployed to Customer Environments shall be provisioned using ephemeral, short-lived credentials or wrapped using Customer-managed keys. Vendor agrees to integrate with Customer KMS/HSM solutions where available and shall provide an option to operate entirely without storing plaintext secret material in any vendor-managed service. Vendor shall provide monthly attestation of compliance and upon Customer request shall provide key rotation logs and audit evidence in machine-readable format."

Operational checklist (for solution engineers/procurement):
- Confirm whether vendor requires persistent secrets storage; if yes, require architecture diagram and justification.
- Require demonstration of agent uninstallability and proof that removal leaves no secrets on disk.
- Require integration test showing SSO + MFA for privileged operations.
- Request past 12 months of third-party pentest summary and remediation plan.
- Validate KMS/HSM integration and a sample key-rotation cycle in staging.

Negotiation guidance for security review panels:
- Push for Customer-managed KMS in all private deployment templates.
- If vendor-managed KMS is unavoidable, require key-wrapping with Customer root and contractually required rotation and export controls.
- Limit retention windows for logs containing metadata about secret usage and ensure logging redaction for sensitive fields.

Open questions / TODOs for legal & product teams:
- Determine acceptable thresholds for automated key rotation frequency defaults (30/90/180 days) and where product needs to expose configuration.
- Confirm whether Customer will allow limited, audited exceptions for short-term local secrets caching to meet latency requirements in certain markets.
- Agree on a standardized machine-readable format for audit exports (suggested: JSONL with schema v1).

Attachments to include with final addendum:
- Architecture diagram template for vendors to complete.
- Audit log schema and example export.
- Checklist for vendor on-boarding for private deployment.
- Example attestation form for deletion and key rotation.

Notes: This is a working draft intended to be attached to vendor MSAs and DPAs as a technical annex. It intentionally errs on the side of prescriptive controls to reduce downstream engineering ambiguity. Please review with legal counsel and product security to align with existing DPA and subprocessor clauses.
